I've read the brief. Here's what it actually requires, kept separate from what I'm inferring.

## Mandatory requirements (stated in the brief)

**Functional**
- A Python program that captures **two audio sources at the same time**: the microphone and the system audio output (the other side of a call).
- The user can **pick the input devices**, from a printed list or with CLI flags.
- **Armenian speech becomes Armenian text**, and each segment is **translated into English**.
- **Speaker labels:** everything from the mic is `Me`. On the system-audio side, different people get `Speaker 1`, `Speaker 2` and so on, and **each person keeps the same label for the whole session**.
- **Live terminal output:** each segment shows the **time, speaker, Armenian text and English text**. The layout is up to you.

**Constraints**
- **≤ 5 s** from the end of a spoken phrase to its English line appearing.
- **Local models only** for speech recognition, translation and diarization. No cloud APIs.
- It must run on the laptop you bring to the interview.
- Models have to be chosen deliberately and justified, since Armenian is low-resource.

## Exclusions (explicitly out of scope)
GUI, installer or packaging, echo handling, recognising speakers by name or across sessions, saving transcripts, any input language other than Armenian. The brief also says that if you have spare time, you should improve reliability rather than add features.

## Deliverables
- A Git repo containing the source code.
- A README covering: setup and run steps including the audio device setup; the chosen models, the alternatives you considered and why; a short architecture description; known limitations and what you'd improve.
- A `chats/` folder with **every** AI session for this project, each as its own unedited `.md` file. **This conversation counts.** They'll also look at the originals in the app, so don't delete any sessions.
- No model weights, audio recordings or API keys in the repo.

## Acceptance criteria (how they evaluate)
- **Live demo:** it runs, the Armenian is recognised, the English is understandable, latency stays ≤ 5 s, and at least 2 call-side speakers are kept apart.
- **Code:** readable, with clear separation of audio, transcription, translation and speaker parts.
- **Process:** how you broke the problem down, what you researched, how you tested assumptions, and whether you steered the AI or just followed it.
- **Honesty:** they explicitly reward stating limits over hiding them.
- **Budget:** about 20 hours of work within one week.

## My assumptions (not in the brief; please correct any of these)
- **System audio on Windows:** WASAPI loopback (e.g. `PyAudioWPatch` or `soundcard`) is the "equivalent" of BlackHole. No virtual cable is needed, and you'll still hear the call normally.
- **Hardware is the main risk.** You have no CUDA GPU and only 8 GB of RAM, so large Whisper models on CPU are probably too slow for 5 s. Realistic candidates are small or medium Whisper variants (ideally Armenian fine-tunes, run with int8 via faster-whisper), or Meta MMS (a CTC model, fast on CPU). For translation, the candidates are NLLB-200-distilled-600M via CTranslate2 or opus-mt-hy-en. I'll benchmark these rather than assume any of them is fast enough.
- **Diarization** will be online: a speaker embedding per segment (e.g. ECAPA) plus incremental clustering, applied **only to the loopback stream**. Full pyannote pipelines are likely too heavy for live use here.
- **Segmentation** will use VAD (Silero) to cut phrases. The "end of phrase" moment that the 5 s budget is measured from is the point where VAD detects silence.
- **Overlapping speech** won't be handled specially. Each segment gets one speaker.
- Iris Xe acceleration (OpenVINO) is an optional optimisation for later, not part of the base design.

## Clarifying questions
These are the only ones that change the architecture or the scope:

1. **Deadline:** when did you receive the brief, and when is the interview? The brief is dated Oct 21, so the remaining time decides how much model benchmarking we can afford.
2. **Dialect:** will the interviewers speak **Eastern Armenian**? Most training data (Common Voice, FLEURS) is Eastern. If Western Armenian might come up, model choice and testing need to cover it.
3. **Call setup for the demo:** will the call side be a real call app (Zoom, Meet, Telegram…) playing through your speakers or headphones, and will you be wearing **headphones**? Without headphones, call audio leaks into the mic. Echo handling is out of scope, but leakage would produce duplicate `Me` lines.
4. **Test audio:** can you record a few short Armenian clips with 2–3 different voices, for local testing only (never committed)? If not, I'll build the tests around public sets like FLEURS `hy_am` and Common Voice.

Once you answer, I'll write `PLAN.md`.

PLAN.md is ready. Three findings shaped it most, and you should check them before we build on them.

**1. The ASR choice has independent backing, but quality is the risk.** The NVIDIA Armenian FastConformer from the Interspeech paper ranks first among open models on ArmBench-ASR, a 2026 benchmark from Metric AI Lab:
- combined WER 19.86, with 7.70 on Common Voice but 60.78 on movie dialogue
- whisper-large-v3 zero-shot, for comparison: 65.12

That gap between read speech and dialogue is the biggest quality risk for a live call, so the plan says this openly instead of promising accuracy.

**2. There's a Windows-friendly way to run that model.** An existing ONNX export runs offline with ONNX Runtime; PyTorch and NeMo are not required. Two catches:
- It uses the CTC head, while the paper reports RNN-T numbers.
- There is no int8 variant.

The model card also says the model is non-streaming, so we transcribe one VAD segment at a time. All of this gets measured in M1 before anything is committed.

**3. Diarization stays simple.** From the diart paper I'm taking only the clustering rules:
- a new-speaker threshold;
- centroids updated only from long-enough segments.

Their segmentation model and tuning pipeline are left out. Newer streaming diarizers like FASTDIAR are listed as a fallback only if measured label accuracy is poor.

**Dialect risk for your mic side.** The benchmark currently covers mainly Eastern Armenian and excludes Western Armenian and regional dialects. So M1 measures your voice separately from Eastern speakers. That's where your recordings come in.

The first step that needs installing anything is M0 (capturing mic and loopback). Tell me when you've reviewed the plan and want to start.

The ASR choice has independent backing, but quality is the risk.** The NVIDIA Armenian FastConformer from the Interspeech paper ranks first among open models on ArmBench-ASR, a 2026 benchmark from Metric AI Lab:\n- combined WER 19.86, with 7.70 on Common Voice but 60.78 on movie dialogue\n- whisper-large-v3 zero-shot, for comparison: 65.12\n\nThat gap between read speech and dialogue is the biggest quality risk for a live call, so the plan says this openly instead of promising accuracy.\n\n**2. There's a Windows-friendly way to run that model.** An existing ONNX export runs offline with ONNX Runtime; PyTorch and NeMo are not required. Two catches:\n- It uses the CTC head, while the paper reports RNN-T numbers.\n- There is no int8 variant.\n\nThe model card also says the model is non-streaming, so we transcribe one VAD segment at a time. All of this gets measured in M1 before anything is committed.\n\n**3. Diarization stays simple.** From the diart paper I'm taking only the clustering rules:\n- a new-speaker threshold;\n- centroids updated only from long-enough segments.\n\nTheir segmentation model and tuning pipeline are left out. Newer streaming diarizers like FASTDIAR are listed as a fallback only if measured label accuracy is poor.\n\n**Dialect risk for your mic side.** The benchmark currently covers mainly Eastern Armenian and excludes Western Armenian and regional dialects. So M1 measures your voice separately from Eastern speakers. That's where your recordings come in.\n\nThe first step that needs installing anything is M0 (capturing mic and loopback). Tell me when you've reviewed the plan and want to start.\n\nSources:\n- [ArmBench-ASR leaderboard](https://metric-ai-armbench-asr.static.hf.space/index.html)\n- [ArmBench-ASR coverage notes (RuntimeWire)](https://runtimewire.com/zh/article/metric-armbench-asr-armenian-speech-benchmark)\n- [nvidia/stt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/stt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc)\n- [OpenVoiceOS ONNX export](https://huggingface.co/OpenVoiceOS/stt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc_onnx)\n- [FASTDIAR](https://microsoft.github.io/fastdiar)\n- [PyAudioWPatch](https://github.com/s0d3s/PyAudioWPatch/)\n- [NLLB CTranslate2 int8](https://huggingface.co/Code-Dev/nllb-200-distilled-600M-ct2-int8)\n- [OpenWHO MT evaluation](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.16048)\n- [Chakmakjian & Wang 2022](https://aclanthology.org/2022.digitam-1.6)",

          "text": "- kazakh\n  - russian\n  - uzbek\n  - english\n  - onnx\npipeline_tag: automatic-speech-recognition\n\nnur-dev/nemo-fast — Multilingual Streaming STT\n\nFastConformer Hybrid CTC+Transducer fine-tuned for Kazakh, Russian, Uzbek, and English. Supports real-time streaming inference via sherpa-onnx or batch inference via NeMo.\n\n\nModel Description\n\nProperty Value\n\nfastconformer_v6.nemo          # Full NeMo model (weights + tokenizer + config)\nonnx/\n  encoder.onnx                 # FastConformer encoder for streaming inference\n  decoder_joint.onnx           # Fused RNN-T decoder+joiner for streaming inference\n\ntranscriptions = model.transcribe([\"audio.wav\"], decoder_type=\"ctc\")\n\nOption B — sherpa-onnx (streaming, CPU or GPU)\n\nInstall\n\npip install sherpa-onnx soundfile numpy\n\nDownload ONNX files\n\n# Using huggingface_hub\nfrom huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download\n\nencoder  = hf_hub_download(\"nur-dev/nemo-fast\", \"onnx/encoder.onnx\")\ndecoder  = hf_hub_download(\"nur-dev/nemo-fast\", \"onnx/decoder_joint.onnx\")\n\nunzip -p fastconformer_v6.nemo vocab.txt > vocab.txt\n\nTranscribe a file (non-streaming)\n\nimport sherpa_onnx\nimport soundfile as sf\nimport numpy as np\n\nrecognizer = sherpa_onnx.OfflineRecognizer.from_transducer(\n    encoder=\"onnx/encoder.onnx\",\n\nReal-time streaming transcription\n\nimport sherpa_onnx\nimport sounddevice as sd\nimport numpy as np\n\nSAMPLE_RATE   = 16000\nCHUNK_MS      = 160          # 160 ms per chunk\nCHUNK_SAMPLES = int(SAMPLE_RATE * CHUNK_MS / 1000)\n\nrecognizer = sherpa_onnx.OnlineRecognizer.from_transducer(\n    encoder=\"onnx/encoder.onnx\",\n    decoder=\"onnx/decoder_joint.onnx\",\n    joiner=\"onnx/decoder_joint.onnx\",\n    tokens=\"vocab.txt\",\n    num_threads=4,\n    sample_rate=SAMPLE_RATE,\n\nThe full server is in the audio-STT repository. Quick start:\n\npip install sherpa-onnx fastapi uvicorn websockets soundfile numpy\n\npython serving/serve_streaming.py \\\n    --encoder  onnx/encoder.onnx \\\n    --decoder  onnx/decoder_joint.onnx \\",

          "text": "Instructions to use OpenVoiceOS/stt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc_onnx with libraries, inference providers, notebooks, and local apps. Follow these links to get started.\n- Libraries\n- NeMo\nHow to use OpenVoiceOS/stt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc_onnx with NeMo:\nimport nemo.collections.asr as nemo_asr asr_model = nemo_asr.models.ASRModel.from_pretrained(\"OpenVoiceOS/stt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc_onnx\") transcriptions = asr_model.transcribe([\"file.wav\"]) - Notebooks\n- Google Colab\n- Kaggle\nstt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc_onnx\nArmenian speech-to-text model. ONNX export of nvidia/stt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc — an NVIDIA NeMo FastConformer-Hybrid CTC model — for onnx-asr. Runs offline with ONNX Runtime; PyTorch and NeMo are not required.\n\nonnx-asr metadata: model_type: nemo-conformer-ctc, features_size: 80, subsampling_factor: 8 |\nThere is no int8 variant: these architectures are convolution-dominated, and\ndynamic quantization produces ConvInteger nodes that ONNX Runtime cannot\nexecute on CPU. int8 requires static QDQ quantization with calibration data.\nUsage\nWith onnx-asr (pip install onnx-asr[cpu,hub]):\nimport onnx_asr\nmodel = onnx_asr.load_model(\"OpenVoiceOS/stt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc_onnx\")\nprint(model.recognize(\"speech.wav\")) # 16 kHz PCM wav\nWith OpenVoiceOS, through\novos-stt-plugin-onnx-asr\n(mycroft.conf):\n{\n\"stt\": {\n\"module\": \"ovos-stt-plugin-onnx-asr\",\n\"ovos-stt-plugin-onnx-asr\": {\n\"model\": \"OpenVoiceOS/stt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc_onnx\"\n}\n}\n}\nExport and verification\nExported from the original checkpoint with NeMo's model.export()\n(CTC decoder head of the hybrid model; see the conversion guide).\n\n- ovos-stt-plugin-onnx-asr — OpenVoiceOS STT plugin\n- NVIDIA NeMo — framework the source model was trained with\n- Downloads last month\n- 1,616\nModel tree for OpenVoiceOS/stt_hy_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pc_onnx\nBase model",

          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Morpheme-Aware Whisper for Low-Resource Armenian ASR\n\nThis model is a fine-tuned version of Whisper Tiny, utilizing a frozen encoder and a custom morpheme tokenizer to achieve cost-effective and accurate speech-to-text for the Armenian language. It outperforms standard OpenAI Whisper models in speed and specific Armenian accuracy by training on the Common Voice 20.0 dataset.\n\nModel Details\n\n  • Model Architecture: Whisper Tiny (Frozen Encoder, Retrained Decoder)\n  • Language: Armenian (hy)\n  • Tokenizer: Custom Morpheme Tokenizer\n  • Dataset: Chillarmo/common_voice_20_armenian\n  • Paper: Morpheme-Aware Whisper for Low-Resource Armenian ASR (Movsesyan, 2025)\n\nAbstract & Motivation\n\nFor a language such as Armenian, having the ability to accurately and cost-effectively translate speech into text is huge. However, due to its low-resource nature, it does not have this yet. This project utilizes Whisper Tiny as the core technology to achieve this goal.\n\nThe problem with current generic models is that they are not robust enough for real-world usage.\n\nThis leads to accessibility issues at events where the speaker is Armenian, but the audience may not fully comprehend the language, forcing them to focus on decoding speech rather than understanding concepts.\n\nEvaluation Results\n\nMetric Value\n\n@inproceedings{movsesyan2025morpheme,\n  author    = {Movses Movsesyan},\n  title     = {Morpheme-Aware Whisper for Low-Resource Armenian ASR},\n  booktitle = {ACM},\n  year      = {2025},\n\nThis model isn't deployed by any Inference Provider. 🙋 Ask for provider support\n\nDataset used to train Chillarmo/Whisper-Tiny-New-Vocab\n\nEvaluation results",

          "text": "Instructions to use BuzzASR/armenian with libraries, inference providers, notebooks, and local apps. Follow these links to get started.\n- Libraries\n- Transformers\nHow to use BuzzASR/armenian with Transformers:\n\nA monolingual automatic speech recognition model for Armenian, fine-tuned from openai/whisper-large-v3. Part of BuzzASR, a suite of 102 language-specialized ASR models (Findings of EMNLP 2026).\nThis model uses full fine-tuning (native per-language tokenizer replacement + text multitask fine-tuning).\n\nResults (normalized CER / WER, %)\n| Test set | CER | WER | Whisper-large-v3 (zero-shot) CER |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| FLEURS | 3.72 | 11.89 | 13.79 |\n| Common Voice 25 | 0.65 | 2.41 | 16.43 |\n| Combined | 2.28 | 7.51 | 15.53 |\n~6.8x CER reduction over Whisper zero-shot on the combined test set.\nUsage\nimport torch, torchaudio\nfrom transformers import WhisperForConditionalGeneration, WhisperProcessor\nmodel = WhisperForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(\"BuzzASR/armenian\", torch_dtype=torch.float16).to(\"cuda\").eval()\nproc = WhisperProcessor.from_pretrained(\"BuzzASR/armenian\")\nwav, sr = torchaudio.load(\"audio.wav\") # 16 kHz mono\n\nThe language/task prompt is baked into the generation config, so no language= argument is needed.\nTraining data\nFLEURS + Common Voice Corpus 25.0 (Mozilla, March 2025; https://commonvoice.mozilla.org/en/datasets), capped per the paper. Text-only data from the Goldfish corpus (Chang et al., 2026).\nLimitations\n\nopenai/whisper-large-v3",

          "text": "Evaluation (from training run)\nMetrics below come from the same validation split used during fine-tuning (auto-generated Trainer card). They are not a fresh benchmark on HyVoxPopuli or Common Voice test sets.\n\nprint(\"Reference:\", sample[\"normalized_text\"])\nPipeline (high level)\nfrom transformers import pipeline\nasr = pipeline(\n\"automatic-speech-recognition\",\nmodel=\"Edmon02/whisper-small-hy\",\ndevice=0,\ngenerate_kwargs={\"language\": \"hy\", \"task\": \"transcribe\"},\n)\nIntended uses\n- Prototyping Armenian ASR in Whisper-based pipelines\n- Comparing Whisper fine-tuning vs MMS / XLS-R on HyVoxPopuli\n- Teaching / reproducing low-resource Whisper fine-tunes\nOut of scope\n- Production transcription without re-benchmarking on your domain\n- Real-time streaming (use faster-whisper + optimized checkpoints after validation)\n- Non-Armenian languages (use base\nopenai/whisper-small or other adapters)\n\n- High WER (~75%) on the recorded validation pass — not competitive with modern MMS adapters\n- Small fine-tuning corpus typical of early experiments\n- Literary / read speech in HyVoxPopuli differs from conversational CV audio — domain shift\n- No word-level timestamps in default\ngenerate config (return_timestamps: false)\n- Multilingual Whisper vocabulary; Armenian uses language token\n<|hy|>\nBias and ethics\nASR errors disproportionately affect dialectal or code-switched Armenian (e.g. Russian lines in literary sources). Do not use outputs for high-stakes decisions without human review.\nCitation\n@misc{whisper_small_hy2024,\nauthor = {Avetisyan, Edmon},\ntitle = {Armenian Whisper Small (whisper-small-hy)},\nyear = {2024},\npublisher = {Hugging Face},\nhowpublished = {\\url{https://huggingface.co/Edmon02/whisper-small-hy}}\n}\nAlso cite OpenAI Whisper and your training data (e.g. Common Voice, HyVoxPopuli).\nLicense\nApache-2.0 (inherits from Whisper fine-tuning convention).           "url": "https://lablab.ai/ai-hackathons/amd-developer-hackathon-act-ii/armenian-asr/armenian-asr-state-of-the-art-speech-recognition",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",
            "site_domain": "lablab.ai",

            "site_name": "lablab"
          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Armenian remains one of the most underserved languages in speech AI. While major languages benefit from massive datasets and highly optimized speech recognition models, Armenian still lacks high-quality open technologies that developers, researchers, and businesses can easily build upon. Our project aims to change that by developing a state-of-the-art Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system specifically for Armenian. The project is built on one of the largest gated Armenian speech datasets available, containing more than 8,000 hours of audio from diverse speakers and recording conditions. We are training and evaluating modern speech recognition models while optimizing every stage of the pipeline, including data preprocessing, audio normalization, fine-tuning, decoding, and inference.\n\nOur long-term vision is to make Armenian one of the best-supported low-resource languages in AI. By improving speech recognition quality and building reliable tooling around it, we hope to accelerate research, enable new AI-powered applications, and strengthen the Armenian AI ecosystem.\nCategory tags:",

          "text": "Metric lanza un benchmark de habla armenia; sistemas cerrados ocupan los primeros ocho lugares\n\nPrimary source: Hugging Face Newsroom\n\nWhy it matters\n\nArmBench-ASR gives Armenian developers a shared test across real speech domains, while showing that closed-model leads shrink or disappear on specific audio types.\n\nA high-contrast photocopy of a research page, showing Armenian script, an audio waveform, and a fragmented film strip with handwritten notes about speech model testing.\n\nEl benchmark inicial v0.1 evalúa cerca de 30 sistemas de pesos abiertos y cerrados usando 10,113 fragmentos de audio que suman aproximadamente 20.7 horas.\n\nLa premisa del benchmark de Metric es sencilla: una sola puntuación limpia de discurso leído no puede mostrar cómo los sistemas de ASR en armenio manejan poesía, medios producidos o noticias narradas.\n\nLos tres conjuntos de datos privados de ArmBench-ASR hacen que el benchmark sea más amplio que una prueba pública de discurso leído.\n\nEl benchmark aún cubre una laguna práctica junto a proyectos amplios como el Open ASR Leaderboard de Hugging Face y baselines multilingües como Whisper de OpenAI.",

          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "#### 3.5 Limitations and Ethical Considerations\n\n#### Data coverage and representativeness\n\nThe NLLB and Western Armenian corpora cover multiple domains, but colloquial speech, code-switching, and low-formality registers remain underrepresented. Consequently, systems may underperform on conversational input and diasporic varieties.\n\n#### Dialect and identity\n\nLevantine Arabic and Western Armenian are diasporic, multi-regional varieties. A single model may unintentionally prefer certain regional lexicons or spellings, which risks marginalizing other communities. Where feasible, future work should stratify evaluation by sub-variety.\n\n#### Licensing and attribution\n\nWe rely on publicly released corpora whose licensing permits research use. However, downstream redistribution of trained models may require additional license checks, especially for subsets with non-commercial clauses.\n\n#### Human evaluation\n\nOur HES is based on three prompts and few raters. While OES mitigates BLEU's brittleness, the human portion is small-scale and subject to annotator bias. Future work should increase rater diversity and adopt MQM-style guidelines.",

          "text": "ԹարգմանիչWestern Armenian and English\n\nVersion 2.0 · hyw ⇆ eng · NLLB-200 distilled, fine-tuned on 1,532,303 sentence pairs\n\nThis is the model from my thesis, running on a shared processor with no graphics card behind it. A short sentence usually comes back in two or three seconds and a paragraph takes longer, though the first request after a quiet spell has to load the model from cold and that one can run to a minute. Nothing is wrong when it does that.\n\nIt runs on the free processor Hugging Face hands out, which is why it sleeps between visitors and wakes up slowly, and getting it onto one that stays awake is what the tin is for: PayPal or Buy Me a Coffee.\n\nԱEnglish ԲԱրեւմտահայերէն\nWas this any good?\nParameters\nAbout this model\n\nThis is the first machine translation system between Western Armenian and English.\n\nThe copyright-free part of the collection is published. The remaining 1,437,035 pairs came from backtranslation, which means taking Western Armenian that nobody ever translated, running it backwards through a model to manufacture an English side, and training on the result. The Armenian in those pairs is writing by actual people and the English is machine output, which is the useful way round, since the thing the model most needs to learn is how to produce Armenian.\n\nIt is better on the kind of prose it was built from: journalism, school material and letters.\n\nNothing you type is stored unless you rate a translation. When you press one of the three buttons, that rating is saved together with your sentence, the translation and the settings it ran with, because rated pairs are where the next version of the corpus comes from. No account, no cookie, nothing else about you.\n\nThere is a Classical Armenian model too, trained the same way. It is paused at the moment while I appeal an automated abuse flag that caught it in a sweep for cryptocurrency miners.\n\nSupported by",

          "text": "Ari Nubar Boyacıoğlu\n2024\nThe First Parallel Corpus and Neural Machine Translation Model of Western Armenian and English\nAri Nubar Boyacıoğlu | Jan Niehues\nProceedings of the 3rd Annual Meeting of the Special Interest Group on Under-resourced Languages @ LREC-COLING 2024\nAri Nubar Boyacıoğlu | Jan Niehues\nProceedings of the 3rd Annual Meeting of the Special Interest Group on Under-resourced Languages @ LREC-COLING 2024\nWestern Armenian is a low-resource language spoken by the Armenian Diaspora residing in various places of the world.           "text": "We focus on a systematic collection of benchmark results with verifiable translation performance and large coverage in terms of languages and domains. The functionalities of the evaluation tool include summaries of benchmarks for over 2,300 models covering 4,560 language directions and 294 languages, as well as the inspection of predicted translations against their human reference. We focus on centralization, reproducibility and coverage of MT evaluation combined with scalability.           "is_missing": false,
          "text": "🌿 Build AI-powered real-time audio applications in a breeze 🌿\nDiart is a python framework to build AI-powered real-time audio applications. Its key feature is the ability to recognize different speakers in real time with state-of-the-art performance, a task commonly known as \"speaker diarization\".\n\nWith diart you can also create your own custom AI pipeline, benchmark it, tune its hyper-parameters, and even serve it on the web using websockets.\nWe provide pre-trained pipelines for:\n- Speaker Diarization\n- Voice Activity Detection\n\nfile for a pre-configured conda environment:\nconda env create -f diart/environment.yml\nconda activate diart\n2) Install the package:\npip install diart\n\nBy default, diart runs a speaker diarization pipeline, equivalent to setting --pipeline SpeakerDiarization\n,\nbut you can also set it to --pipeline VoiceActivityDetection\n. See diart.stream -h\nfor more options.\nUse StreamingInference\n\nsegmentation = m.SegmentationModel.from_pretrained(\"model_name\")\nembedding = m.EmbeddingModel.from_pretrained(\"model_name\")\nBelow is a list of all the models currently supported by diart:\nModel Name | Model Type | CPU Time* | GPU Time* |\n\nThe latency of segmentation models is measured in a VAD pipeline (5s chunks).\nThe latency of embedding models is measured in a diarization pipeline using pyannote/segmentation\n(also 5s chunks).\n* CPU: AMD Ryzen 9 - GPU: RTX 4060 Max-Q\n\nStreaming is powered by RxPY, but the blocks\nmodule is completely independent and can be used separately.\nObtain overlap-aware speaker embeddings from a microphone stream:\nimport rx.operators as ops\nimport diart.operators as dops\n\nWe propose to address online speaker diarization as a combination of incremental clustering and local diarization applied to a rolling buffer updated every 500ms.\n\nDiart aims to be lightweight and capable of real-time streaming in practical scenarios. Its performance is very close to what is reported in the paper (and sometimes even a bit better).",

          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "# HIGHLY EFFICIENT REAL-TIME STREAMING AND FULLY ON-DEVICE SPEAKER DIARIZATION WITH MULTI-STAGE CLUSTERING\n\n**Quan Wang\\* Yiling Huang\\* Han Lu Guanlong Zhao Ignacio Lopez Moreno** Google LLC, USA \\*Equal contribution\n\n{quanw, yilinghuang, luha, guanlongzhao, elnota}@google.com\n\n# **ABSTRACT**\n\nWhile recent research advances in speaker diarization mostly focus on improving the quality of diarization results, there is also an increasing interest in improving the efficiency of diarization systems. In this paper, we demonstrate that a multi-stage clustering strategy that uses different clustering algorithms for input of different lengths can address multi-faceted challenges of on-device speaker diarization applications.\n\nBoth the main clusterer and the pre-clusterer can be configured with an upper bound of the computational complexity to adapt to devices with different resource constraints. This multi-stage clustering strategy is critical for streaming on-device speaker diarization systems, where the budgets of CPU, memory and battery are tight.",

          "text": "FASTDIAR\n\nFrame-Level Speaker Encoder for Streaming Diarization\n\nView the Project on GitHub microsoft/fastdiar\n\nFASTDIAR: Frame-Level Speaker Encoder for Streaming Diarization\n\narXiv paper GitHub code HuggingFace demo\n\nFASTDIAR is a streaming diarization architecture with a confidence-gated online clustering at a fixed 960 ms delay, which is the most accurate streaming diarizer on low-overlap benchmarks, degrades far less than cache-based systems beyond four speakers, and needs no diarization corpus in training.\n\n  • Frame-level streaming encoder: A state-of-the-art speaker recognition model, ReDimNet2, made causal and stripped of temporal pooling.\n\nEvery label leaves the system at a fixed 960 ms delay.\n  • Fast on CPU: With 10.4M parameters, the full system (encoder, VAD and clustering) runs 5× faster than real time on a single CPU thread.\n\nResults\n\nDiarization error rate (DER, %) with a collar of 0 and overlapped speech excluded, split by the number of speakers. Streaming Sortformer is capped at four speakers, so the three corpora that cross that boundary are also split at it. RTF is measured on one CPU thread. Bold marks the lowest DER in each column.\n\nModel #Params Latency\n(ms)\nRTF NOTSOFAR VoxConverse DIHARD3 AMI RAMC\n≤4≥5all ≤4≥5all ≤4≥5all 3–4 2\ndiart 5.8M10000.16 42.5654.1648.01 12.8117.1716.12 17.4046.1422.04 28.79 25.87\nStreaming Sortformer 117.7M10401.54 14.4833.4523.39 5.4123.5519.15 14.0834.2517.34 25.56 25.27\n\nFrame-to-frame cosine similarity of the same excerpt. Left: the baseline, offline ReDimNet2-B6 run on 2-second chunks with an 80 ms shift to simulate streaming. Right: the proposed frame-level encoder.\n\ntitle={{FASTDIAR}: Frame-Level Speaker Encoder for Streaming Diarization},\n  author={Torgashov, Nikita and K{\\\"o}p{\\\"u}kl{\\\"u}, Okan},\n  journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.02941},\n  year={2026}\n}",

          "text": "Skip to main content\n\nA python framework to build AI for real-time speech\n\nProject description\n\n🌿 Build AI-powered real-time audio applications in a breeze 🌿\n\nPyPI Version PyPI Downloads Python Versions Code size in bytes License\n\nThe pipeline diart.SpeakerDiarization combines a speaker segmentation and a speaker embedding model to power an incremental clustering algorithm that gets more accurate as the conversation progresses:\n\nUse StreamingInference to run a pipeline on an audio source and write the results to disk:\n\nfrom diart import SpeakerDiarization\nfrom diart.sources import MicrophoneAudioSource\nfrom diart.inference import StreamingInference\n\nModel Name Model Type CPU Time* GPU Time*\n🤗 pyannote/segmentation (default) segmentation 12ms 8ms\n🤗 pyannote/segmentation-3.0 segmentation 11ms 8ms\n🤗 pyannote/embedding (default) embedding 26ms 12ms\n\nFor a more advanced usage, diart also provides building blocks that can be combined to create your own pipeline. Streaming is powered by RxPY, but the blocks module is completely independent and can be used separately.\n\nExample\n\nObtain overlap-aware speaker embeddings from a microphone stream:\n\nimport rx.operators as ops\nimport diart.operators as dops\nfrom diart.sources import MicrophoneAudioSource, FileAudioSource\n\nDiart is also compatible with the WebSocket protocol to serve pipelines on the web.\n\nFrom the command line\n\ndiart.serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 7007\ndiart.client microphone --host <server-address> --port 7007\n\nfrom diart import SpeakerDiarization\nfrom diart.sources import WebSocketAudioSource\nfrom diart.inference import StreamingInference\n\npipeline = SpeakerDiarization()\nsource = WebSocketAudioSource(pipeline.config.sample_rate, \"localhost\", 7007)\n\nDiart is the official implementation of the paper Overlap-aware low-latency online speaker diarization based on end-to-end local segmentation by Juan Manuel Coria, Hervé Bredin, Sahar Ghannay and Sophie Rosset.",

          "text": "Abstract\nThis manuscript deals with the task of real-time speaker diarization (SD) for stream-wise data processing.\n\nThe described scheme yields results similar to the reference offline system while operating solely on a CPU with a low real-time factor (RTF) below 0.1 and a constant latency of around 5.5 s. In the next part of the work, our research moves toward much more demanding and complex real-time processing of audio-visual data streams.\n\nIt yields diarization error rates that are competitive with the existing state-of-the-art offline audio-visual methods while allowing us to process various audio-video streams, e.g., from Internet or TV broadcasts, in real-time using GPU and with\n\nThe requirements on the properties of streaming SD systems are different and much more restricted than those on the offline version. The most critical factor in many real-time applications is that of the computational demands.\n\nThe diarization system employed in our platform, therefore, must work in a real-time mode with a constant delay when processing live streams as well as recordings created offline.\n\nOur practical experience thus shows that low computational requirements and CPU-only operation in a production still pay off in the case of real-time processing.\nTherefore, in this paper, we first propose a new lightweight SD method that allows us to process infinite streams of acoustic data and satisfies all of the above-mentioned requirements: it runs in a real-time mode solely utilizing a CPU and operates\n\nNote that this part of the present manuscript represents an extension of our previous work [2].\nThis work’s second main contribution lies in extending our method toward much more complex real-time processing of audio-visual data streams.\n\nA novel lightweight approach to speaker diarization is proposed, allowing for real-time processing of audio streams.\n-\nOur scheme operates with a low real-time factor and latency solely on a CPU but wi",

          "text": "diart  by juanmc2005\n\nReal-time audio applications framework\n\nCreated 4 years ago\n1,936 stars\n\nTop 22.2% on SourcePulse\n\nGitHubView on GitHub\nProject Summary\n\nDiart is a Python framework for building real-time AI-powered audio applications, specializing in speaker diarization.\n\nDiart combines speaker segmentation and speaker embedding models within an incremental clustering algorithm. This approach refines accuracy as a conversation progresses. The framework supports custom AI pipelines, hyper-parameter tuning, and web serving. It is built upon pyannote.audio models, leveraging their segmentation and embedding capabilities for efficient and accurate speaker diarization.\n\nQuick Start & Requirements\n\n  • Installation: pip install diart\n  • Prerequisites: ffmpeg < 4.4, portaudio == 19.6.X, libsndfile >= 1.2.2. A Conda environment file (environment.yml) is provided for easier setup.\n\n• Resources: Supports CPU and GPU (RTX 4060 Max-Q tested). Latency benchmarks provided for various models.\n  • Documentation: Links to installation, streaming, models, tuning, pipelines, WebSockets, and research papers are available within the README.\n\nHighlighted Details\n\n  • Supports real-time streaming from microphones or audio files.\n\nTranscription and speaker-aware transcription features are listed as \"coming soon.\" Reproducing exact benchmark results may require specific versions of pyannote.audio.\n\nHealth Check\nLast Commit\n\n1 year ago\n\nResponsiveness\n\nInactive\n\nawesome-diarization by wq2012\n\n0.2%\n2k\nList of resources for speaker diarization\nCreated 7 years ago\nUpdated 7 months ago\nFeedback?           "text": "Towards a Unified ASR System for the Armenian Standards\n\nSamuel Chakmakjian1,2, Ilaine Wang2\n1SeDyL (CNRS-Inalco), 2ERTIM (Inalco)\n\n7 rue Guy Môquet 94800 Villejuif, 2 rue de Lille 75007 Paris\n{samuel.chakmakjian, ilaine.wang}@inalco.fr\n\nAbstract\n\nSpeech Recognition (ASR) technologies.         {
          "type": "knowledge",
          "title": "whats the difference between western armenian and eastern armenian",
          "url": "https://strommeninc.com/whats-the-difference-between-western-armenian-and-eastern-armenian/",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",
            "site_domain": "strommeninc.com",
            "favicon_url": "https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=64&domain=strommeninc.com",
            "site_name": "strommeninc"
          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Yes, Armenian is a single language with two main branches: Eastern Armenian and Western Armenian.\n\nWhether you’re learning to connect with family, heritage, or culture, knowing which dialect you’re engaging with is the first step to mastering the Armenian language.\n\nWestern Armenian and Eastern Armenian\n\nWhat Is Eastern Armenian?\n\nThough Eastern and Western Armenian share the same alphabet, Eastern Armenian uses a reformed orthography, introduced during the Soviet era. This makes its spelling and pronunciation slightly more streamlined compared to its Western counterpart.\n\nUnlike Eastern Armenian, which is rooted in modern-day Armenia, Western Armenian is a diasporic dialect, rich in heritage, resilience, and cultural memory.\n\nMain Characteristics\n\nWestern Armenian differs from its Eastern counterpart in a few important ways:\n\n  • Pronunciation: Uses harder consonants. For example, where Eastern Armenian uses b, d, and g, Western Armenian often uses p, t, and k.\n\nKey Differences Between Eastern and Western Armenian\n\nWhile Eastern and Western Armenian share the same roots and alphabet, they have developed distinct differences over centuries, shaped by geography, history, and cultural influences.\n\n• Eastern Armenian uses softer consonant sounds. For example, the letters that sound like b, d, and g in Eastern Armenian often correspond to p, t, and k sounds in Western Armenian.\n  • Western Armenian tends to have harder, more aspirated consonants, making the dialect sound sharper to Eastern Armenian speakers.\n\n2. Vocabulary\n\nBoth dialects have unique vocabulary influenced by different neighboring cultures:\n\n• Eastern Armenian is ideal if you want to explore contemporary Armenian culture, literature, music, and modern media.\n  • Western Armenian is perfect for those interested in preserving Armenian heritage, diaspora history, and classical literature.",

          "title": "Metric lanza un benchmark de habla armenia; sistemas cerrados ocupan los primeros ocho lugares",
          "url": "https://runtimewire.com/es/article/metric-armbench-asr-armenian-speech-benchmark",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",
            "site_domain": "runtimewire.com",
            "favicon_url": "https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=64&domain=runtimewire.com",
            "site_name": "runtimewire"
          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Metric lanza un benchmark de habla armenia; sistemas cerrados ocupan los primeros ocho lugares\n\nHrant Davtyan, fundador y CEO de Metric, publicó ArmBench-ASR el 20 de agosto, ofreciendo al reconocimiento de voz en armenio una prueba común a través de discurso leído, poesía, diálogos de películas y noticas narradas.\n\nLa premisa del benchmark de Metric es sencilla: una sola puntuación limpia de discurso leído no puede mostrar cómo los sistemas de ASR en armenio manejan poesía, medios producidos o noticias narradas. Evaluaciones públicas con frecuencia cubren un único estilo de habla, usan un procesamiento de texto inconsistente o carecen de procedimientos estandarizados. ArmBench-ASR aplica el mismo marco de evaluación en cinco dominios.\n\nArmBench-ASR convierte ese compromiso en algo contra lo que otros creadores de modelos pueden medir sus sistemas.\n\nCinco conjuntos de datos exponen cinco problemas diferentes\n\nArmBench-ASR usa el mismo material fijo y reglas de procesamiento para cada sistema evaluado.\n\nLos tres conjuntos de datos privados de ArmBench-ASR hacen que el benchmark sea más amplio que una prueba pública de discurso leído.\n\nArmBench-ASR usó parámetros por defecto, con la temperatura de Gemini ajustada a cero y el modo \"thinking\" deshabilitado o mantenido en un ajuste mínimo.\n\nEl benchmark aún cubre una laguna práctica junto a proyectos amplios como el Open ASR Leaderboard de Hugging Face y baselines multilingües como Whisper de OpenAI.\n\nMetric ha estado construyendo un marco de evaluación más amplio para el armenio, incluyendo proyectos ArmBench para modelos de lenguaje y embeddings de texto.\n\nArmBench-ASR extiende ese programa de investigación al habla al tiempo que expone dónde radica el siguiente trabajo.",

        {
          "type": "knowledge",
          "title": "Metric releases Armenian speech benchmark; closed systems take first eight spots",
          "url": "https://runtimewire.com/article/metric-armbench-asr-armenian-speech-benchmark",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",
            "site_domain": "runtimewire.com",
            "favicon_url": "https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=64&domain=runtimewire.com",
            "site_name": "runtimewire"
          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Metric releases Armenian speech benchmark; closed systems take first eight spots\n\nHrant Davtyan's lab tested nearly 30 systems on 20.7 hours of Armenian audio across five speech datasets, with closed systems leading the combined ranking.\n\nHrant Davtyan, founder and CEO of Metric, released ArmBench-ASR on August 20, giving Armenian speech recognition a common test across read speech, poetry, movie dialogue and narrated news.\n\nMetric's benchmark premise is straightforward: a single clean read-speech score cannot show how Armenian ASR systems handle poetry, produced media, or narrated news.\n\nArmBench-ASR turns that commitment into something other model builders can measure against.\n\nFive datasets expose five different problems\n\nArmBench-ASR uses the same fixed material and processing rules for every evaluated system.\n\nMetric says it manually reviewed and corrected the reference transcripts for all three.\n\nThe interactive leaderboard breaks results out by dataset and lets users compare strict and normalized word and character error rates.\n\nIt also warns buyers against treating a single leaderboard percentage as a complete description of transcription quality.\n\nMetric reports that every evaluated model recorded its highest strict WER on the private Movies collection.\n\nArmBench-ASR's three private datasets make the benchmark broader than a public read-speech test. Their absence from the release also prevents outside researchers from fully reproducing the most distinctive portion of the evaluation.\n\nThe benchmark still fills a practical gap beside broad projects such as Hugging Face's Open ASR Leaderboard and multilingual baselines such as OpenAI's Whisper. General-purpose evaluations can show whether a speech model travels across languages.\n\nMetric has been building a wider Armenian evaluation stack, including ArmBench projects for language models and text embeddings.\n\nArmBench-ASR extends that research program into speech while exposing where the next work lies.",
          "is_citable": true,
          "prompt_context_metadata": {
            "search_provider": "anthropic",
            "url": "https://runtimewire.com/article/metric-armbench-asr-armenian-speech-benchmark"
          },
          "links": null
        },
        {
          "type": "knowledge",
          "title": "Metric 发布亚美尼亚语语音基准测试;封闭系统占据前八名",
          "url": "https://runtimewire.com/zh/article/metric-armbench-asr-armenian-speech-benchmark",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",
            "site_domain": "runtimewire.com",
            "favicon_url": "https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=64&domain=runtimewire.com",
            "site_name": "runtimewire"
          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "ArmBench-ASR gives Armenian developers a shared test across real speech domains, while showing that closed-model leads shrink or disappear on specific audio types.\n\nMetric 的亚美尼亚语工作属于自筹资金的研究路线。在其研究页面中,Metric 表示其研究人员投入自己的时间和预算,因为即便短期商业回报不足,亚美尼亚语 AI 基础设施仍然重要。ArmBench-ASR 将这种承诺转化为其他模型开发者可以度量的基线。\n\n五个数据集揭示五种不同的问题\n\nArmBench-ASR 对每个被评估系统使用相同的固定材料和处理规则。其两个公开组成部分是 Common Voice 26,一个众包朗读语音集,以及 Google 的 FLEURS 的亚美尼亚语测试拆分。Metric 在手动审查 FLEURS 抄本后发布了一小批更正\n\nArmBench-ASR 的三个私有数据集使得基准比公开朗读测试更广泛。它们在发布中缺失也阻止了外部研究人员完全复现评估中最具特色的部分。\n\nMetric 直接说明了这一限制。当前套件主要覆盖东亚美尼亚语,排除了西亚美尼亚语和地区方言。它测试转录准确性,但不衡量说话人分离(speaker diarization)、词级时间戳、流式处理、长篇行为或下游性能。评估于 2026 年 7 月下旬和 8 月上旬进行,因此托管系统以后可能通过未版本化的模型更新或路由决策发生变化。\n\n这对封闭 API 的影响最大。在相同产品名称下的未来重跑可能对应不同的底层模型。ArmBench-ASR 使用了默认参数,将 Gemini 的 temperature 设置为 0,并将“思考”禁用或保持在最低设置。这些选择使得此次发布成为对已配置服务的时点比较,而非永久性的排名。\n\n该基准仍然在诸如 Hugging Face 的 Open ASR Leaderboard 以及像 OpenAI 的 Whisper 这样的多语种基线项目之外填补了一个实用空白。通用评估可以展示一个语音模型能否跨语言适用。Davtyan 与 Metric 所问的是亚美尼亚语开发者真正面临的更狭窄问题:当说话者不再朗读一条干净的测试句子而电影开始时会发生什么。\n\nArmBench-ASR 将该研究计划扩展到语音领域,同时揭示了下一步工作的方向。Metric 计划添加代码切换、非正式对话、采访、通话、会议、重叠说话者、专有词汇、说话人分离和时间戳质量等测试。每一项新增都提高了收集和验证参考数据的成本,尤其是对于一个缺乏标准化数据的语言而言。\n\nDavtyan 的赌注是:缺失的基础设施无论如何都值得去构建。首次发布为亚美尼亚语模型开发者提供了一个基线和一组具有挑战性的音频领域,也为资金最充足的语音提供商提供了一个超出另一个干净朗读集的测试。",
          "is_citable": true,
          "prompt_context_metadata": {
            "search_provider": "anthropic",
            "url": "https://runtimewire.com/zh/article/metric-armbench-asr-armenian-speech-benchmark"
          },
          "links": null
        },
        {

          "title": "huggingface armbench asr a benchmark for armenian asr",
          "url": "https://www.plushcap.com/content/huggingface/blog/huggingface-armbench-asr-a-benchmark-for-armenian-asr",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",

            "site_name": "plushcap"
          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Home / Companies / Hugging Face / Blog / Post Details\nContent Deep Dive\n\nArmBench-ASR: A Benchmark for Armenian ASR\n\nBlog post from Hugging Face\n\nPost Details\nCompany\nDate Published\nAuthor\nAlexander Shahramanyan, Mariam Avetisyan, and Hrant Davtyan\n\nArmBench-ASR v0.1 is a benchmark designed to make Armenian automatic speech recognition systems easier to compare by evaluating nearly 30 open-weight and closed models across 10,113 audio clips, totaling about 20.7 hours, from five datasets\n\nThe benchmark is primarily focused on Eastern Armenian, includes three private datasets that limit full reproducibility, and measures transcription accuracy rather than features such as diarization, timestamps, or long-form performance.",
          "is_citable": true,
          "prompt_context_metadata": {
            "search_provider": "anthropic",
            "url": "https://www.plushcap.com/content/huggingface/blog/huggingface-armbench-asr-a-benchmark-for-armenian-asr"
          },
          "links": null
        },
        {
          "type": "knowledge",
          "title": "metric armbench asr armenian speech benchmark",
          "url": "https://runtimewire.com/ja/article/metric-armbench-asr-armenian-speech-benchmark",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",
            "site_domain": "runtimewire.com",
            "favicon_url": "https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=64&domain=runtimewire.com",
            "site_name": "runtimewire"
          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Metric のベンチマークの前提は単純だ:単一のクリーンな朗読スコアだけでは、アルメニア語の ASR システムが詩や制作されたメディア、ナレーション付きニュースをどのように扱うかを示せない。公開評価はしばしば単一の話法にとどまり、テキスト処理が一貫しなかったり標準化された手順が欠けていたりする。ArmBench-ASR は同じ評価フレームワークを5つのドメインに渡って適用する。\n\nMetric は三つのプライベートコレクションを追加した。Poems はバックグラウンドミュージックを伴う表現豊かな文学朗読を含む。Movies は会話形式の台詞と制作されたメディアのノイズを含む。Infocom は一人の話者が朗読するアルメニア語のニュース原稿で構成される。Metric はこれら三つすべての参照トランスクリプトを手作業でレビューし訂正したと述べている。\n\ninteractive leaderboard はデータセットごとに結果を分解し、厳密および正規化された単語誤り率と文字誤り率を比較できるようにしている。厳密なスコアリングは句読点や大文字小文字への感度を保持する。正規化スコアリングはテキストを小文字化し、参照とモデル出力の両方に対して一貫した Unicode、スペーシング、文字処理ルールを適用した後で句読点を除去する。\n\nArmBench-ASR の三つのプライベートデータセットは、このベンチマークを公開朗読テストよりも広いものにしている。同時に、それらがリリースに含まれていないことで、外部の研究者が評価のもっとも特徴的な部分を完全に再現することを妨げている。\n\nMetric は言語モデルやテキスト埋め込み向けの ArmBench プロジェクトを含め、より広いアルメニア語評価スタックを構築してきた。SmartGateVC は 2021 年の Metric のプレシードラウンドに出資しており、当時 Metric はかつて Pinsight として知られた応用 AI 研究ラボと説明されていた。金額や評価額は公表されていない。",
          "is_citable": true,
          "prompt_context_metadata": {
            "search_provider": "anthropic",
            "url": "https://runtimewire.com/ja/article/metric-armbench-asr-armenian-speech-benchmark"
          },
          "links": null
        },

          "text": "ArmBench-LLM 1.0: Benchmarking LLMs on Armenian Language Tasks\n\nCommunity Article\nPublished April 2, 2026\n\nFollowing our recent release of ArmBench-TextEmbed (and the ATE-2 models), as well as our latest publication at the LoResLM 2026 EACL workshop, Metric AI Lab is thrilled to announce the next major leap in our non-commercial Armenian AI initiative: ArmBench-LLM 1.0.\n\nLast year, we introduced ArmBench-LLM 0.1 (legacy), which laid the groundwork by evaluating LLM knowledge using translated MMLU-PRO subsets and Armenian University Exams.\n\nNote: Open-source models under 30B parameters were evaluated locally to minimize API spend.\n\n๐Ÿ“Š Leaderboard (Top 10)\n\nNote: size is not reported for propriatory models. image\n\nFull leaderboard + per-task breakdown available in the HF Space.\n\nKey Findings & Leaderboard Insights\n\n  1. Gemini 3 is still the king Google's gemini-3-flash-preview secured the #1 rank with an Average score of 0.6350. Surprisingly, it is also one of the most cost-effective models on the market.\n\nBeyond the main leaderboard, here are specialized insights that can be crucial if you are building a product with a very specific focus:\n\n• Reliability-Based Exclusions (Claude 4.5/4.6): To maintain the highest standards of benchmark integrity, we have excluded Claude 4.5 and 4.6 models from the current leaderboard.\n\nIf you are using Grok via the UI, you will likely find the Armenian language experience to be significantly more robust and reliable than the current benchmark scores might suggest.",

          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "# From Zero to Hero: An Open LLM Ecosystem for Armenian\n###### Abstract\nArmSTEM is a parallel English–Armenian collection of 373K math and science problems, 324K of them with step-by-step solutions, translated into Armenian and verified through both answer-preserving LLM judgment and human evaluation.\n\n*Gemma tokens* use the stock Gemma-4 vocabulary (4.15 tokens per Armenian word, Table 13), the unit the released model was trained in, so all corpus sizes, mixture shares, and cross-corpus comparisons use them, with other public corpora re-tokenized by us.\n\n| Variant | our-iid | our-tail | FW2-test | hyWiki | LR-Sum | FLORES | Avg |\n\nTable 5 gives the resulting composition, totalling 372,907 pairs, about 311M Armenian and 124M parallel English Gemma tokens.\n\n## 3 Adapting Gemma-4 to Armenian\n\n#### Training on our datasets produces the best open Armenian model.\narm-gemma-e4b reaches a suite mean of 0.50, above the unadapted Gemma-4-E4B at 0.48 and above every existing open Armenian model, whose means range from 0.35 to 0.47 (Figure 1, Table 8).\n\n#### Existing Armenian models show the same trade at scale.\n\nArmenianGPT-1.0-3B, the strongest existing open model at a mean of 0.47, still trails even the unadapted Gemma-4-E4B at 0.48.\n\nMadlad-400: A multilingual and document-level large audited dataset.\n\n| Gemma-3 / Gemma-4 | 4.15 | 3.42 |\n\nThe CPT runs other than STEM-CPT-full used a 109,885-item subset of ArmSTEM (7,404 GSM8K, 48,584 AceReason-Math, 45,883 OpenScience, 8,014 OSR-2), about 59M Armenian and 24M parallel English Gemma tokens, so the 4%/2% mixture shares give",

This means that among open weight models, NLLB-54B is still the preferred choice.\n\n# OpenWHO: A Document-Level Parallel Corpus for Health Translation in Low-Resource Languages\n\n##### Models\nOur model selection is designed to compare modern LLMs (both open and closed weights) against conventional NMT baselines. For NMT baselines, we select NLLB-200 (3.3B & 54B, Costa-jussà et al., 2024) and MADLAD-400 10B Kudugunta et al.\n\n| Armenian (hye) | Armenian | 125 | 1982 |\n\n| Model | mkd  | kaz  | kat  | hye  | aze  | sqi  | tet  | som  | sin  | AVG  |\n\n| NLLB-200 3.3B | 43.85 / 3.52  | 63.35 / 3.17  | 58.39 / 3.09  | 51.59 / 3.16  | 52.17 / 4.62  | 53.87 / 3.51  |\n| NLLB-200 54B | 45.52 / 3.38  | 58.39 / 3.23  | 59.80 / 2.78  | 53.18 / 2.8  | 51.02 / 5.07  | 53.58 / 3.45  |\n| MADLAD-400 10B | 40.68 / 3.98  | 38.24 / 5.69  | 59.40 / 2.88  | 47.38 / 5.38  | 46.02 / 7.1  | 46.34 / 5.01  |\n| Gemma-3 27B | 45.14 / 2.99  | 43.95 / 5.93  | 59.55 / 2.50  | 52.36 / 2.62  | 52.56 / 3.83  | 50.71 / 3.61  |\n\n| NLLB-200 3.3B | 30.74 / 7.85  | 46.51 / 4.99  | 47.29 / 4.80  | 42.17 / 5.44  | 45.16 / 6.29  | 42.37 / 5.87  |\n| NLLB-200 54B | 30.91 / 7.99  | 46.55 / 4.92  | 48.63 / 4.57  | 44.27 / 4.93  | 44.64 / 6.74  | 43.00 / 5.83  |\n| MADLAD-400 10B | 27.44 / 9.21  | 35.42 / 6.76  | 47.38 / 4.75  | 37.73 / 7.02  | 38.67 / 7.94  | 37.33 / 7.14  |\n| Gemma-3 27B | 38.29 / 4.59  | 38.26 / 6.71  | 54.98 / 3.45  | 47.94 / 3.89  | 47.93 / 5.24  | 45.48 / 5.26  |",

          "title": "Multilingual Machine Translation with Open Large Language Models at",
          "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.02481",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",
            "site_domain": "arxiv.org",
            "favicon_url": "https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=64&domain=arxiv.org",
            "site_name": "arxiv"
          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Multilingual Machine Translation with Open Large Language Models at.\n\nIn this paper, we systematically explore\n\nthe abilities of open LLMs with less than ten billion parameters to handle multilingual machine\n\ntranslation (MT) tasks. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on six popular LLMs and find\n\nthat models like Gemma2-9B exhibit impressive multilingual translation capabilities.\n\n**3.1** **Datasets**\n\nWe evaluate the multilingual translation performance on the FLORES-200 (Team et al., 2022)\n\nbenchmark.\n\n• NLLB-54.5B: The largest and best multilingual NMT model with encoder-decoder architecture released by the No Language Left Behind\n\n(NLLB) project (Team et al., 2022).\n\nFor the FLORES-200 benchmark, we evaluate\n\nWe conduct our experiments on the FLORES-200 devtest dataset, which includes 1012 sentences for each language.\n\nFigure 1: The tokenizer efficiency of open-source LLMs for each non-English language.\n\nModel WMT-24 FLORES-200\n\n**4.2** **In-context Multilingual Translation** translation capability.\n\n**Performance with Open LLMs**\n\nWe here investigate the multilingual translation\n\nlearning strategies on the FLORES-200 and WMT-24 benchmarks. For each open LLM, we report\n\nits translation performance across 28 languages\n\nwith five randomly selected translation pairs^9^ from\n\nWe then illustrate the translation performance on\n\nthe FLORES-200 benchmark according to varying\n\n1 to 5, and the translation performance plateaus\n\nFigure 2: MT performance on the FLORES-200 benchmark with different numbers of in-context exemplars.\n\n**Translation with Gemma Models**",
          "is_citable": true,

          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "In this work, we introduced TranslateGemma, a. series of open models based on Gemma 3, specifi-. cally enhanced for machine translation. … Madlad-400: A multilingual and. document-level large audited dataset. vances in Neural Information ...\n\n**We present TranslateGemma, a suite of open machine translation models based on the Gemma 3**\n\n**foundation models.           "is_missing": false,
          "text": "# The Ongiini-Eval-OW Benchmark: A Concept Paper for the Planned Benchmarking of Machine Translation and Large Language Models on Oshindonga and Oshikwanyama\n\n# Sebastian Küpers\\*\n\n#### **Abstract**\n\nMajor commercial services (Google Translate, DeepL, Microsoft Translator), open multilingual MT models (NLLB-200, MADLAD-400), and the open Masakhane checkpoint collection all lack coverage of either standardised dialect, Oshindonga or Oshikwanvama. We announce **Ongiini-Eval-OW**.\n\nFor a language community of this size, the absence of any public machinetranslation evaluation benchmark is striking.\n\nWe have directly inspected the tokenizer of NLLB-200 (NLLB Team et al., 2022), the README and supportedlanguage list of MADLAD-400 (Kudugunta et al., 2023), and the public Masakhane checkpoint repositories, and found no Oshiwambo coverage in any of them.\n\nFrontier large language models — Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, Qwen — do produce Oshiwambo-like output when prompted, but the quality has not been measured by any benchmark and is therefore neither defensible nor falsifiable.\n\nThis paper announces **Ongiini-Eval-OW**, a planned 600-item evaluation benchmark for English $\\leftrightarrow$ Oshindonga and English $\\leftrightarrow$ Oshikwanyama machine translation and large-language-model output.\n\n# 2 Background: the Oshiwambo translation gap\n\nWhen the translation layer is absent, the entire\n\nTable 1: The two standardised Oshiwambo dialects covered by this benchmark.\n\n| NLLB-200 (NLLB Team et al., 2022) | No | Inspected special_tokens_map.json on Hugging Face; no Oshiwambo language code present | |",
          "is_citable": true,
          "prompt_context_metadata": {
            "search_provider": "anthropic",
            "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.31727"
          },

          "text": "This fork will allow you to use the WASAPI device as loopback using PyAudio.\nSo you can use speakers to record audio β¨\nIf you want to record sound from speakers in python, then this fork is for you.\nPyAudioW(indows|ASAPI)Patch come only with WMME, DirectX and WASAPI support if you need more -> create an issue\nThe Windows Audio Session API (WASAPI) allows you to use output devices (that support this API) in loopback mode. At the time of release, it was impossible to achieve this using the original version of PyAudio.\nNote: Now WASAPI loopback devices are duplicated at the end of the list as virtual devices. That is, to record from speakers, you need to use not just a WASAPI device, but its loopback analogue. All loopback devices are input devices.\n\n- Ability to record audio from WASAPI loopback devices (see example)\n-\nnew methods:\nget_host_api_info_generator\n- Iterate over all Host APIsget_device_info_generator\n- Iterate over all devicesget_device_info_generator_by_host_api\n- Iterate over all devices, by specific Host API(index/type)get_loopback_device_info_generator\n- Iterate over all devices(with loopback mode)print_detailed_system_info\n- Print some info about Host Api and devicesget_default_wasapi_loopback\n- Returnloopback\nfor default speakersget_wasapi_loopback_analogue_by_index\n- Returnloopback\nfor device via indexget_wasapi_loopback_analogue_by_dict\n- Returnloopback\nfor device related toinfo_dict\nget_default_wasapi_device\n- Return default (out/in)put device forWASAPI\ndriver\n-\nnew features:\n- Context manager support, for PyAudio(manager) and Stream classes\n- Run\npython -m pyaudiowpatch\nto get list of devices(likeprint_detailed_system_info\ncall)\n\nPyAudio provides Python bindings for PortAudio v19, the cross-platform audio I/O library. With PyAudio, you can easily use Python to play and record audio on a variety of platforms, such as GNU/Linux, Microsoft Windows, and Apple macOS.",

          "text": "PortAudio fork with WASAPI loopback support\nProject description\nPyAudioWPatch\nThis fork will allow you to use the WASAPI device as loopback using PyAudio.\nSo you can use speakers to record audioвњЁ\nFor whom?\nIf you want to record sound from speakers in python, then this fork is for you.\nPyAudioW(indows|ASAPI)Patch come only with WMME, DirectX and WASAPI support if you need more -> create an issue\nHow\n\n- Print some info about Host Api and devicesget_default_wasapi_loopback\n- Returnloopback\nfor default speakersget_wasapi_loopback_analogue_by_index\n- Returnloopback\nfor device via indexget_wasapi_loopback_analogue_by_dict\n- Returnloopback\n\nto get list of devices(likeprint_detailed_system_info\ncall)\nExamples:\n- Play sine, using 'new context manager'\n- Record audio from default speakers\n- Simple recording app\n- Cross-platform concept (Not example)\nSources\n\nPyAudio is distributed under the MIT License.\nInstallation\nSee the INSTALLATION file in the source distribution for details. In summary, install PyAudio using pip\non most platforms.\nWindows\npython -m pip install pyaudio\nThis installs the precompiled PyAudio library with PortAudio v19 19.7.0 included. The library is compiled with support for Windows MME API, DirectSound, WASAPI, and WDM-KS. It does not include support for ASIO.\n\nFile details\nDetails for the file PyAudioWPatch-0.2.12.6-cp312-cp312-win32.whl\n.\nFile metadata\n- Download URL: PyAudioWPatch-0.2.12.6-cp312-cp312-win32.whl\n- Upload date:\n- Size: 84.2 kB\n- Tags: CPython 3.12, Windows x86\n\nFile details\nDetails for the file PyAudioWPatch-0.2.12.6-cp311-cp311-win32.whl\n.\nFile metadata\n- Download URL: PyAudioWPatch-0.2.12.6-cp311-cp311-win32.whl\n- Upload date:\n- Size: 84.1 kB\n- Tags: CPython 3.11, Windows x86\n\nFile details\nDetails for the file PyAudioWPatch-0.2.12.6-cp310-cp310-win32.whl\n.\nFile metadata\n- Download URL: PyAudioWPatch-0.2.12.6-cp310-cp310-win32.whl\n- Upload date:\n- Size: 84.0 kB\n- Tags: CPython 3.10, Windows x86",

          "text": "PortAudio fork with WASAPI loopback support\nProject description\n❤ Recall.ai - API for desktop recording\n\nIf you want to record sound from speakers in python, then this fork is for you. You can get recording from any device that supports WASAPI, for example, you can even record audio from Bluetooth headphones🎧\n\nimport pyaudiowpatch as pyaudio\nwith pyaudio.PyAudio() as p:\n# Open PyA manager via context manager\nwith p.open(...) as stream:\n# Open audio stream via context manager\n# Do some stuff\n...\nOr in original PyAudio way:\nimport pyaudiowpatch as pyaudio\n\n- Fixed problem with name encoding\n- Ability to record audio from WASAPI loopback devices (see example)\nMore detailed\n-\nnew methods:\n\nindexget_wasapi_loopback_analogue_by_dict- Returnloopbackfor device related toinfo_dictget_default_wasapi_device- Return default (out/in)put device forWASAPIdriver\n-\nnew features:\n- Context manager support, for PyAudio(manager) and Stream classes\n- Run\npython -m pyaudiowpatchto get list of devices(likeprint_detailed_system_infocall)\nExamples:\n- 🆕 Sequential recording from speakers\n- Play sine, using 'new context manager'\n- Record audio from default speakers\n- Simple recording app\n\nInstallpython- run in the PyAudioWPatch directory:\npython setup.py install\n- ???\n- Profit.\nAlso you can build wheels:\npip install cibuildwheel- Run in Cygwin:\n./cygwin_cibuildwheel_build.sh\n- Get your wheels in the\n./wheelhousefolder\nPyAudio\n\nDetails for the file pyaudiowpatch-0.2.12.8-cp314-cp314-win_amd64.whl.\nFile metadata\n- Download URL: pyaudiowpatch-0.2.12.8-cp314-cp314-win_amd64.whl\n- Upload date:\n- Size: 101.0 kB\n- Tags: CPython 3.14, Windows x86-64\n\nDetails for the file pyaudiowpatch-0.2.12.8-cp313-cp313-win_amd64.whl.\nFile metadata\n- Download URL: pyaudiowpatch-0.2.12.8-cp313-cp313-win_amd64.whl\n- Upload date:\n- Size: 99.3 kB\n- Tags: CPython 3.13, Windows x86-64",

          "text": "Skip to content\n\nomerbb/vis\n\nRepository files navigation\n\nTerminal Audio Visualizers (WASAPI Loopback)\n\nA small collection of terminal-based audio visualizers for Windows. Most scripts can capture system audio via WASAPI loopback (using PyAudioWPatch). Some scripts may fall back to microphone input if loopback is unavailable.\n\nTip: Run the launcher first: vis_ui.py.\n\nFeatures\n\n  • Multiple visualizer modes (spectrum-like, oscilloscope/XY, circular, EEG-style, fire effect, etc.)\n  • Windows system-audio capture via WASAPI loopback (PyAudioWPatch)\n  • Terminal UI (ANSI colors via colorama)\n\nRequirements\n\n  • Windows 10/11 recommended (WASAPI loopback)\n  • Python 3.9+ (3.10+ recommended)\n\nPython packages\n\nInstall dependencies:\n\npip install numpy colorama PyAudioWPatch\n\nUse the on-screen controls to select and start a visualizer.\n\n2) Run a visualizer directly\n\npython vis.py\npython vis_os.py\npython vis_fire.py\npython vis_circular.py\npython vis_circular_braile.py\npython vis_eeg.py\npython vis_eeg_central.py\n\nControls\n\npip install PyAudioWPatch\n\nLoopback device list is empty / loopback not found\n\n  • Make sure you’re on Windows.\n  • Ensure audio is playing on the default output device.\n\nThe XY visualizer needs two channels. Try a stereo output device, or disable “mono audio” in Windows accessibility settings.\n\nNotes\n\n  • These are terminal visualizers; performance depends on terminal rendering speed.\n  • WASAPI loopback is Windows-specific; non-Windows behavior may be limited or may require microphone input.\n\nLicense\n\nMIT License\n\nAI-Assisted Development Disclosure\n\nTerminal-based audio visualizer suite for Windows (WASAPI loopback via PyAudioWPatch) with a unified TUI manager—spectrum analyzer, circular/XY scopes, fire and EEG-style effects, plus one-command CLI install (vis).\n\nResources\n\nLicense\n\nStars",

          "url": "https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/discussions/windows11/any-good-audio-recorder-for-windows-11-pc%EF%BC%9F/4555523/replies/4555534",
          "metadata": {

          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Forum Discussion\nAny good audio recorder for Windows 11 PC?\nPyAudioWPatch is a fantastic obscure and free method for capturing system audio on Windows. It is exactly the kind of complex, code-based approach you were asking for. It essentially gives you the raw tools to build your own audio recorder for Windows 11 PC without relying on a pre-packaged application.\nBefore you proceed, be aware of these specifics:\n- No Standalone App: PyAudioWPatch is a library, not a finished product. You are building the audio recorder for Windows 11 PC functionality yourself.\n- The \"Loopback\" Quirk: On Windows, your speakers appear twice in the device list: once as an output, and once as a virtual input (the loopback version). Your code must specifically target this loopback input device.\n- Helper Method: The library provides get_default_wasapi_loopback() to simplify finding the correct device for your default speakers.\nHere is a simplified look at the core logic you would use. This is not a complete script, but it shows the essential steps for your custom audio recorder for Windows 11 PC:\nimport pyaudiowpatch as pyaudio\nimport wavewith pyaudio.PyAudio() as p:\n# 1. Find the loopback device for your default speakers\nloopback_device = p.get_default_wasapi_loopback()\n# 2. Configure the stream using the device's native format\nstream = p.open(\nformat=pyaudio.paInt16,\nchannels=loopback_device['maxInputChannels'],\nrate=int(loopback_device['defaultSampleRate']),\ninput=True,\ninput_device_index=loopback_device['index']\n)\nFor the full implementation, you would refer to the pawprecord wasapi_ loopback.py example in the project's GitHub repository.",

          "title": "FASTDIAR: Frame-level speaker encoder for Streaming Diarization",
          "url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.02941",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",
            "site_domain": "arxiv.org",
            "favicon_url": "https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=64&domain=arxiv.org",

          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "# FASTDIAR: FRAME-LEVEL SPEAKER ENCODER FOR STREAMING DIARIZATION\n\nNikita Torgashov\\*\n\nOkan Köpüklü\n\nDepartment of Speech, Music and Hearing KTH Royal Institute of Technology Stockholm, Sweden\n\nMicrosoft Munich, Germany\n\n#### **ABSTRACT**\n\nMost systems apply an utterance-level speaker encoder to short, heavily overlapping chunks, which wastes computation and leaves the model optimized for the wrong task. We instead turn a state-of-the-art speaker recognition architecture into a causal frame-level encoder that reads the stream once and emits one embedding every 80 ms from a bounded two-second window of past audio, and pair it with online clustering\n\nlatency, degrades far less than cache-based systems as the number of speakers grows, and runs five times faster than real time on a single CPU thread.\n\n*Index Terms*— Speaker Diarization, Speaker Recognition, Streaming Speaker Diarization\n\nMost diarization systems are built around a speaker encoder [1, 2], applied off the shelf to short, heavily overlapping chunks.\n\nTwo works reach frame rate: [15] distils an utterance-level teacher into a student that pools over a centred window, and LS-EEND [16, 17] learns a causal frame-wise encoder jointly with its attractor decoder. Neither gives a streaming encoder with a bounded past: the first reads the future, the second carries the whole recording in its recurrent state.\n\nIn this work we present FASTDIAR (FrAme-level speaker encoder for STreaming DIARization). Our contributions are (i) a causal frame-level speaker encoder that needs no chunking, no temporal pooling and no recomputation, and summarizes a two-second past window, (ii) an extension of incremental online clustering where an\n\nCode and models are available at https://github.com/microsoft/fastdiar.\n\n<sup>\\*</sup>Work done during internship at Microsoft.\n\n#### 2. METHOD\n\n## 2.1. Streaming speaker encoder\n\nWe address three properties of this design that conflict with streaming diarization.",

          "text": "Skip to content\n\nReleases: microsoft/fastdiar\n\nRelease list\n\nv0.1.0\n\nChoose a tag to compare\n\n@herimor herimor released this 03 Oct 08:23\ne7f9bbc\n\nFirst release of FASTDIAR: streaming speaker diarization with a fixed 960 ms delay.\n\nIncludes inference, benchmarking, and training code, plus pre-trained checkpoints of the streaming encoder:\n\nModel Checkpoint Parameters\nsmall fastdiar-small-90be5da5.pt 2.4 M\nmedium fastdiar-medium-32df7509.pt 4.6 M\nlarge (default) fastdiar-large-f6d71444.pt 10.4 M\n\nThe checkpoints are downloaded automatically on first use; see the README for usage.",

          "text": "FASTDIAR\n\nFrame-Level Speaker Encoder for Streaming Diarization\n\nView the Project on GitHub microsoft/fastdiar\n\nFASTDIAR: Frame-Level Speaker Encoder for Streaming Diarization\n\narXiv paper GitHub code HuggingFace demo\n\n1Department of Speech, Music and Hearing, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden\n2Microsoft, Munich, Germany\n*Work done during an internship at Microsoft.\nFASTDIAR online clustering running frame by frame on a recording\n\nOverview\n\nFASTDIAR is a streaming diarization architecture with a confidence-gated online clustering at a fixed 960 ms delay, which is the most accurate streaming diarizer on low-overlap benchmarks, degrades far less than cache-based systems beyond four speakers, and needs no diarization corpus in training.\n\n  • Frame-level streaming encoder: A state-of-the-art speaker recognition model, ReDimNet2, made causal and stripped of temporal pooling.\n\nFASTDIAR 10.4M9600.19 19.2324.2521.58 10.7012.8812.35 24.7332.9526.06 22.15 21.61\n\nAblations\n\nConfidence score detects cluster borders\n\nLeft: confidence score over an 18-second excerpt, dropping at each speaker change. Right: frame-to-frame cosine similarity matrix of the same excerpt.\n\nFrames below the threshold (dashed line) are still labeled, but only confident frames update a speaker centroid, so embeddings from a speaker change never blur two clusters together.\n\nFrame-level encoder forms sharper clusters\n\nFrame-to-frame cosine similarity matrices of the baseline chunk-based encoder (left) and the proposed frame-level encoder (right).\nFrame-to-frame cosine similarity of the same excerpt. Left: the baseline, offline ReDimNet2-B6 run on 2-second chunks with an 80 ms shift to simulate streaming. Right: the proposed frame-level encoder.\n\ntitle={{FASTDIAR}: Frame-Level Speaker Encoder for Streaming Diarization},\n  author={Torgashov, Nikita and K{\\\"o}p{\\\"u}kl{\\\"u}, Okan},\n  journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.02941},\n  year={2026}\n}",

        {
          "type": "knowledge",
          "title": "sigport.org",
          "url": "https://sigport.org/sites/all/modules/pubdlcnt/pubdlcnt.php?fid=9466",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",
            "site_domain": "sigport.org",
            "favicon_url": "https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=64&domain=sigport.org",
            "site_name": "sigport"
          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Topic Streaming Speaker Diarization: answering \"who speaks when\"\nin streaming applications\nMethod Deep-learning based streaming speaker diarization with frame-wise\nattractors\n\n• Frame-wisely detect a flexible number of speakers and extract/update\ntheir corresponding attractors.\n\n• A look-ahead mechanism allows leveraging some future frames.\nNetwork\n\n• A causal speaker embedding encoder by masked self-attention module.\n• Look-ahead with 1-dimensional convolution.\n• An online attractor decoder to extract frame-wise attractors.\n\nContributions\n• Excellent speaker diarization performance on both simulated dataset\n\nand real-world CALLHOME data.\n• Computational cost is lower compared to block-wise online methods.\n\nNetwork Architecture\nThe basic strategy is to design\n✓ a causal speaker embedding encoder: masked\n\nself-attention and Conv1D along time dimension.\n✓ an online attractor decoder: extract attractors\n\nframe-wisely and is realized with a non-autoregressive\nself-attention network.\n\nLinear\nIn: T×(S+2)×2D\n\nMasked Frame Self-Attention Module\n\nCross-Attractor Self-Attention Module\n\nAttractor Decoder\n\n×MFeed Forward \n\nSigmoid\n\n: concatenation operation\n\n𝒆𝑡𝒆1 𝒆𝑇… …𝒙𝑡𝒙1 𝒙𝑇… … Audio  Features\n\n𝒂𝒔,𝑡𝒂𝑠,1 𝒂𝑠,𝑇… …\nS+2Attractors\n\n𝒆𝑡𝒆1 𝒆𝑇… …ෝ𝒚𝑡ෝ𝒚1 ෝ𝒚𝑇… … Diarization Results\n\nS+2\n\nC\n\nExtract/update frame-\n\nwise attractors.\n\nDistinguish different \n\nattractors at each frame.\n\nMaintain attractor \n\nconsistency of each speaker.\n\nCausally extract frame-wise \n\nspeaker embeddings.\n\nExploit some future frames. \n\nFigure: Architecture of the proposed FS-EEND system.\n\nExperiments\n\nDataset\n\n• FS-EEND processes audio stream and performs diarization\nframe by frame, with a causal embedding encoder and an\nonline attractor decoder.\n\n• FS-EEND shows superiority in diarization performance,\nsystem latency, and computational complexity.\n\nCodea\nahttps://github.com/Audio-WestlakeU/FS-EEND",

          "prompt_context_metadata": {

        {
          "type": "knowledge",
          "title": "Frame-wise streaming end-to-end speaker diarization with non-autoregressive self-attention-based attractors",
          "url": "https://astro.paperswithcode.com/paper/frame-wise-streaming-end-to-end-speaker",
          "metadata": {
            "type": "webpage_metadata",
            "site_domain": "paperswithcode.com",
            "favicon_url": "https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?sz=64&domain=paperswithcode.com",
            "site_name": "paperswithcode"
          },
          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Frame-wise streaming end-to-end speaker diarization with non-autoregressive self-attention-based attractors\nThis work proposes a frame-wise online/streaming end-to-end neural diarization (FS-EEND) method in a frame-in-frame-out fashion. To frame-wisely detect a flexible number of speakers and extract/update their corresponding attractors, we propose to leverage a causal speaker embedding encoder and an online non-autoregressive self-attention-based attractor decoder. A look-ahead mechanism is adopted to allow leveraging some future frames for effectively detecting new speakers in real time and adaptively updating speaker attractors. The proposed method processes the audio stream frame by frame, and has a low inference latency caused by the look-ahead frames. Experiments show that, compared with the recently proposed block-wise online methods, our method FS-EEND achieves state-of-the-art diarization results, with a low inference latency and computational cost.\nPDF Abstract",

          "title": "Speaker Diarization",
          "url": "https://localai.io/features/audio-diarization/index.html",
          "metadata": {

          "is_missing": false,
          "text": "Speaker Diarization\n\nSpeaker diarization answers the question “who spoke when?” — given an audio clip with multiple speakers, it returns time-stamped segments labelled with a stable speaker ID (SPEAKER_00, SPEAKER_01, …).\n\n• sherpa-onnx — pyannote-3.0 segmentation + a speaker-embedding extractor (3D-Speaker, NeMo, WeSpeaker) + fast clustering. Pure diarization — no transcription cost. Recommended when you only need speaker turns.\n\n{\"id\": 0, \"speaker\": \"SPEAKER_00\", \"label\": \"0\", \"start\": 0.00, \"end\": 2.34},\n    {\"id\": 1, \"speaker\": \"SPEAKER_01\", \"label\": \"1\", \"start\": 2.34, \"end\": 4.10}\n  ]\n}\n\n{\"id\": 0, \"speaker\": \"SPEAKER_00\", \"label\": \"0\", \"start\": 0.00, \"end\": 2.34, \"text\": \"Hello, world.\"},\n    {\"id\": 1, \"speaker\": \"SPEAKER_01\", \"label\": \"1\", \"start\": 2.34, \"end\": 4.10, \"text\": \"How are you?\"}\n  ],\n  \"speakers\": [\n\nQuick start\n\ncurl http://localhost:8080/v1/audio/diarization \\\n  -H \"Content-Type: multipart/form-data\" \\\n  -F file=\"@meeting.wav\" \\\n  -F model=\"pyannote-diarization\" \\\n  -F num_speakers=3\n\nBackend setup — sherpa-onnx (pure diarization)\n\nSherpa-onnx needs two ONNX models: pyannote segmentation and a speaker-embedding extractor. Place them under your LocalAI models directory and reference them from the YAML:\n\nname: pyannote-diarization\nbackend: sherpa-onnx\ntype: diarization\nparameters:\n  model: sherpa-onnx-pyannote-segmentation-3-0/model.onnx\noptions:\n  - diarize.embedding_model=3dspeaker_speech_campplus_sv_zh-cn_16k-common.onnx\n  # Optional clustering knobs (per-call DiarizeRequest fields override these):\n\n• Speaker identity across files: speaker IDs (SPEAKER_00, SPEAKER_01, …) are local to each request. To track the same person across multiple recordings, combine /v1/audio/diarization with /v1/voice/embed (speaker embedding) and maintain your own embedding store.\n\n• Sample rate: input is automatically converted to 16 kHz mono via ffmpeg before the backend sees it; sherpa-onnx pyannote-3.0 requires 16 kHz.",
